tool.name: fasta_uppercase
tool.description: upper-case a FASTA, discarding any pre-existing soft-masking

param.name: input
param.label: Assembly FASTA
param.help: Plain or gzipped. Soft-masked or not.

tool.help:
**fasta_uppercase** — rewrites every sequence line in upper case and leaves header lines exactly as they are.
The lower-case tally uses ``gsub(/[a-z]/, "&")``, which replaces each match with itself and returns the count, so the line is unchanged and counting costs no second pass.
**Header lines are never modified**, and that is the whole correctness argument for the tool. Sequence names are case-sensitive identifiers, so a blanket ``tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'`` renames every scaffold — ``scaffold_12`` becomes ``SCAFFOLD_12`` — and every downstream join by name then silently finds nothing.
**Why WF-B needs it.** Each masker already upper-cases its own private working copy, so the BED tracks were always computed de novo. ``bedtools maskfasta -soft``, however, lower-cases the union intervals *on top of whatever was already lower-case*. Applied to an assembly that arrives soft-masked, the published soft-masked FASTA becomes the union of this pipeline's mask and the assembly's own, with no way to tell them apart, while the BED tracks report only the former.
**This panel is such a case**, and the evidence is in this repository rather than elsewhere. In the captured WF-B run — invocation ``75ed0631e40c6c7b``, ``workflows/examples/wf_b_examples.json`` — PvP01 arrives already soft-masked: its 880-base input peek is **75.9%** lower-case, and the same peek of the published ``maskfasta`` output is **91.6%**, with no position reverted to upper case. This workflow's own union for PvP01, genome-wide, is **39.01%** (that run's ``masking_table``). So the FASTA it published carried mostly the mask the assembly came with, while the BED tracks beside it described only the 39.01%.
*(The 75.9 / 91.6 pair is measured on that one captured peek, not genome-wide; it establishes the direction and the mechanism, and the union figure is the genome-wide one.)*
